The Bushveld elephant shrew (Elephantulus intufi) is a small insectivorous mammal endemic to southern African savannas, whose life history presents a fascinating blend of traits typical of small-bodied afrotherians. Basal metabolic rate, measured through respirometry, stands at 52.03 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 52.03 milliliters of oxygen per hour] under thermoneutral conditions at 30.9 °C [T = 30.9 °C], a value that is consistent with the moderate metabolic demands of a mammal weighing only a few tens of grams. Females give birth to altricial neonates that weigh roughly 10 grams [Wwb = roughly 10 grams], a modest birth mass that necessitates an extended period of maternal investment. The gestation period lasts approximately 51 days [tg = approximately 51 days], with this duration recorded under a controlled thermal environment of 35.3 °C [T = 35.3 °C], and reported values in the literature cluster tightly between 50 and 52 days. This relatively long gestation for an animal of this body size likely reflects the complex placental development characteristic of the Afrotheria.

Reproductive output in bushveld elephant shrews is modest but consistent, constrained by both litter size and the frequency of breeding events. Each litter typically contains 1 to 2 young per litter [N_R_i = 1 to 2 young per litter], and females are capable of producing an estimated 5 litters per year [F_R_i = 5 litters per year], based on field observations and captive colony data. This annual reproductive rate is maintained under typical active-body temperatures of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C], which corresponds to the species' euthermic core temperature. The weaning process marks a significant energetic transition, with offspring reaching nutritional independence at a wet weight of 29 grams [Wwx = 29 grams]. Maternal provisioning during the suckling stage is intensive, as the pups must more than double their birth mass to achieve this weaning weight before transitioning to a diet of invertebrates.

Developmental milestones in Elephantulus intufi are precisely timed and closely tied to thermal physiology. At the species' normothermic body temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C], the time from birth to weaning is 28 days [tx = 28 days], a developmental period that falls within the three-to-four week range reported for related elephant-shrew species. During this pre-weaning interval, the altricial neonates undergo rapid organogenesis and begin to exhibit the characteristic probing foraging behavior of adult elephant shrews. The transition to a fully independent juvenile stage is marked by the attainment of this weaning mass, after which the growing animals must learn to capture small arthropods on their own. This relatively short weaning period, combined with the high metabolic costs of lactation, places considerable energetic demands on the mother, who must maintain her own body condition while supporting the rapid growth of her litter.

Sexual maturation in this species occurs considerably later than weaning, reflecting a slow pace of life for a mammal of this size. Puberty is reached at 330 days after birth [tp = 330 days after birth], a duration that is maintained under the species' active thermoregulatory set point of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C]. This prolonged juvenile phase is unusual among small-bodied insectivores and likely relates to the complex cognitive and physical skills required for successful foraging in the rocky, semi-arid habitats the bushveld elephant shrew occupies. During this sub-adult stage, individuals continue to refine their locomotor abilities and expand their home ranges, gradually attaining the body mass and physiological condition necessary for reproductive competition. The delay in achieving reproductive maturity is also reflected in the species' maximum lifespan, with one captive specimen documented to have survived for 4.2 years [am = 4.2 years] under standard vivarium conditions at 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C], suggesting that this species follows a relatively slow life-history trajectory for its body size.

Adult body mass exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in Elephantulus intufi, consistent with patterns observed across the Macroscelididae. Females ultimately attain a larger adult body mass, with a maximum recorded wet weight of 52 grams [Wwi = 52 grams], though the range for adult females generally spans from 40 to 74 grams. Males are distinctly smaller, reaching a maximum adult wet weight of 45 grams [Wwi = 45 grams], with a documented range of 35 to 56 grams. This size differential may relate to the energetic demands of gestation and lactation, as larger females are better able to sustain the costs of producing and provisioning litters over the course of the breeding season. Comparisons with the closely related Elephantulus myurus and Elephantulus rupestris show that these body masses are within the typical range for the genus, though the upper limits in both sexes are notably higher than those recorded for some desert-dwelling congeners. The species thus exhibits a pattern of moderate sexual size dimorphism that aligns with its polygynous or promiscuous mating system.
